title: Causal Detection of Multi-Step LLM Agent Attacks
pdf_path: papers/Causal Detection of Multi-Step LLM Agent Attacks.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker embeds instructions in external content observed by an agent and relies on multi-step propagation to a sensitive sink; individual actions look legitimate. CausalTrace audits complete logged trajectories after the fact rather than intercepting live execution. The attacker cannot modify the user task, system prompt, or agent code.
core_contributions: Reframes multi-step prompt-injection detection as causal inference over agent trajectories
Builds Structural Causal Models with data-dependency, trust-transfer, and state-enablement edges
Uses Pearl's do-calculus and Probability of Necessity to ask whether harm would occur if the injection were blocked
Combines semantic routing, GNN/RF classifiers, taint/watermark signals, and counterfactual scores in a five-way ensemble
Bidirectional slicing recovers attack chains and bottlenecks
Reports 99.2% F1 on semi-real data, 92.6% F1 OOD, and a 1,077,298-trajectory benchmark
limitations: Post-hoc audit requiring complete trajectories, not real-time prevention
Causal estimates rely on additive noise, correct structural equations, and no hidden confounding
LLM router early-exit is a single point of failure and is not adversarially evaluated
Causal module's marginal contribution is small in-distribution (99.2 vs 99.1/99.0)
No adaptive attacker despite the threat model listing cloaking and evasion
Dataset accounting inconsistencies: Table 9 vs 11, ToolEmu 1,072 vs 947, CausalBench 49,898 vs >1M
Unkeyed SHA-256 provenance marker is not authentication
theoretical_crypto_links: None; SCM, do-calculus, and Probability of Necessity are causal inference, not cryptographic proof
Unkeyed SHA-256 is used only as a marker label, not a commitment, MAC, or signature
applied_crypto_links: Only incidental unkeyed SHA-256; no signatures, MACs, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed/Merkle audit logs and logger attestation are our inference; they protect record integrity, not causal correctness
evidence_refs: pp.15-21 marker design, dataset composition, and task-conditioned experiment

title: Learning When to Act or Refuse: Guarding Agentic Reasoning Models for Safe Multi-Step Tool Use
pdf_path: papers/Learning When to Act or Refuse_Guarding Agentic Reasoning Models for Safe Multi-Step Tool Use.pdf
threat_model_summary: An agent may cause irreversible harm while planning or calling tools on malicious or adversarial tasks. MOSAIC trains the policy to insert explicit safety checks and to refuse as a first-class action. Evaluation uses static ASB/AgentHarm/PrivacyLens tasks; no adaptive attacker targets the safety-check mechanism.
core_contributions: MOSAIC: plan, optional safety check, then act or refuse as a learnable loop
Pairwise trajectory preferences from an LLM judge, aggregated into a group-relative reward and optimized with GRPO
Safety thoughts and refusal become explicit, first-class actions
Reports harm reduction, injection robustness, privacy leakage reduction, and utility/token efficiency across four open models
GPT-4o/5 with safety scaffolding show large harm reductions without weight training
limitations: No adaptive attacker against safety thoughts or refusal
Safety thoughts are generated by the same policy and are not verified for faithfulness
Judge reward can be Goodharted; judge prompt penalizes safe completion
Phi-4 shows a safety regression (harm 0.06 to 0.09, DPI ASR 0.19 to 0.28)
Only three model families; no prior-defense quantitative baselines
No external enforcement layer, code, or checkpoints
Several internal inconsistencies in token percentages, NR columns, and benchmark naming
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Safety is operationalized by behavioral benchmark metrics
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, capability tokens, or audit logs
A tool-gateway enforcement layer is our inference; refusal remains a voluntary model action
evidence_refs: pp.3-4 MOSAIC loop and preference RL
pp.5-7 main results, privacy, token use
pp.20-22 additional tables and judge replacement

title: A-MemGuard: A Proactive Defense Framework For LLM-Based Agent Memory
pdf_path: papers/A-MemGuard_A Proactive Defense Framework For LLM-Based Agent Memory.pdf
threat_model_summary: An adversary injects seemingly benign records into an agent's memory, either through limited direct write access or indirectly through benign queries that cause archival. The malicious effect activates only under a trigger query, and the corrupted outcome can be stored as precedent. A-MemGuard filters at retrieval time; it does not authenticate writers.
core_contributions: A-MemGuard: retrieve K memories, generate a structured reasoning path per memory, and use an LLM judge to synthesize a consensus plan
Flags paths inconsistent with the consensus or unsafe, and filters their memories
Distills anomalous paths into a separate lesson memory that is retrieved before future actions
AgentPoison ASR-r 100 to 2.13 and ASR-a 87.23 to 6.38 on EHRAgent
MINJA indirect injection ASR 0.667 to 0.256 (GPT-4o-mini) and 0.633 to 0.233 (LLaMA)
limitations: Retrieval-time filtering only; poisoned records remain in main memory
No writer authentication or provenance
Lesson memory is a new attack surface and is not sanitized or signed
LLM judge can itself be prompt-injected
Consensus paths are generated by the same model and are not independent
No false-positive/over-blocking metric; ASR-t remains 36-43%
Headline >95% applies to ASR-r, not end-to-end ASR-t
Internal inconsistencies: EntityOverlap Jaccard 15.0, lesson synthesis wording, K=4 vs 7 paths
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'consensus' is semantic agreement among LLM-generated paths, not Byzantine consensus
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed memory provenance and Merkle logs are our inference; they detect unauthorized modification but not authorized malicious writes
evidence_refs: pp.24-26 ASR-t gap, malicious-majority filtering, limitations

title: SkillTrojan: Backdoor Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/SkillTrojan_Backdoor Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker publishes seemingly benign skills. After installation the attacker has no host access; malicious behavior is triggered by a user query and reconstructed from payload fragments emitted by multiple legitimate-looking skill invocations, then executed as a side effect inside the skill runtime.
core_contributions: SkillTrojan: a backdoor that targets skill implementations rather than model weights or training data
Splits an encoded payload across multiple benign-looking skill actions and reassembles it via a verifier skill
Supports automated synthesis of backdoored skills from arbitrary templates
Releases SkillTrojanX with 3,000+ backdoored skills, 1,200 templates, four payload families, and 50 triggers
Reports 97.2% ASR with 89.3% ACC on GPT-5.2 and 98.2%/99.4% safe verdicts from two LLM scanners
limitations: 'Encryption' is XOR plus Base64; the key is distributed with the verifier skill, so it is white-box obfuscation, not cryptography
Qwen3-VL is a counterexample: ASR 26.7 below AgentPoison 37.6 and ACC 48.4 below non-attack 53.2
No confidence intervals, seeds, or repeated runs
Baselines are restricted to transient channels and require an extra payload tool, so capabilities are not equal
Only two LLM static scanners evaluated; proposed sandbox/provenance defenses are not prototyped
Dataset coverage is sparse relative to the configuration space
Signed package provenance cannot stop composition of individually legitimate skills
theoretical_crypto_links: None; XOR plus Base64 is not a cryptographic construction and has no confidentiality definition
No security game, theorem, reduction, or IND-CPA-style claim
applied_crypto_links: Nominal only: 'encryption' is obfuscation with a bundled key
Signed skill provenance authenticates publishers but not behavior; capability sandboxing is the closer system-level mitigation and is not cryptographic
evidence_refs: pp.3-5 threat model and payload partition/reassembly
pp.6-9 main results, scanner evasion, crypto ablation
pp.12-14 algorithm, baseline adaptation, additional results

title: When Agents Go Rogue: Activation-Based Detection of Malicious Behaviors in Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/When Agents Go Rogue_Activation-Based Detection of Malicious Behaviors in Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: One or more agents in a multi-agent system are compromised through prompt injection, memory poisoning, or tool attacks, and malicious behavior can propagate along communication edges. AcMAS reads each local agent's final-layer activation and flags deviations from a benign prototype. Attacks are static and not adapted to the detector.
core_contributions: AcMAS: activation-space one-class detection for malicious agents in synchronous and asynchronous MAS
Uses the final-layer last-token hidden state, a normalized benign centroid, and a cosine-distance threshold
Synchronous MAS uses momentum prototype updates; asynchronous MAS uses a fixed prototype
Replaces isolation with activation correction toward the normal prototype and regeneration
Detection F1 0.92-0.95 versus G-Safeguard 0.72 synchronous and 0.43 asynchronous
AUROC 97.58-99.48 and low detection overhead (about 0.22% inference time)
limitations: Requires white-box access to internal activations and runtime hooks; closed APIs are out of scope
Thresholds are calibrated on labeled validation data, so the method is not fully unsupervised
Prototype poisoning and domain shift are acknowledged but not solved
No adaptive attacker that gradually drifts activations
No text-embedding control to isolate the benefit of internal activations
Activation correction may erase role/task-specific information; no human evaluation
Privacy claim is unsupported; activations may leak input information
Internal inconsistencies in asynchronous baseline and HotPotQA numbers
theoretical_crypto_links: None; activation anomaly detection is not authentication or integrity attestation
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, OAuth, or capability tokens
TEE attestation, signed audit logs, and capability-gated correction are our inference; they protect execution/log integrity, not semantic detection correctness
evidence_refs: pp.4-6 activation extraction, prototype, threshold, correction
pp.18-20 threshold calibration, cross-domain results, task performance
